comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
Fixed on branch `drift-fd2b-eebc`, commit `d043be48dcba`, pushed for review with `jaded-pugnacious-isopod` (they share `.github/workflows/terraform-drift.yml`, so they are one change).

## Scope decision: SPLIT INTO JOBS, not reorder

The ticket offered two defensible options (reorder plan-before-fmt, or `continue-on-error` + a later gate). I took a third that dominates both: `terraform fmt -check` moved into its own top-level job `fmt`, with **no `needs:` relationship** to the `plan` job.

Reasoning, against the ACs:

- **AC1** — reordering satisfies it only for the *first* failure. Within one job, a fmt failure still fails the job that carries the drift verdict, and a later maintainer re-ordering steps re-creates the bug. Separate jobs make the coupling structurally absent rather than conventionally avoided.
- **AC2** — `continue-on-error` would have made the fmt failure non-fatal, which is the same "reported as success" shape this ticket is about. Its own job fails outright instead. A test asserts no fmt step carries `continue-on-error`.
- **AC3** — this is what actually decided it. Reordering leaves ONE job name carrying both outcomes, so "whitespace is wrong" and "we did not look for drift" remain indistinguishable in the checks list without opening logs. Two jobs make a red run self-describing: `fmt` red = whitespace, `plan` red = drift (or an unprovable tree).
- **AC4** — `tests/unit/test_terraform_drift_workflow_shape.py` parses the workflow and pins: no fmt step shares the plan job; the plan job does not `needs:` any fmt job; fmt survives with `-check` and without `continue-on-error`; fmt and plan are distinct job names. It was RED on the pre-fix workflow for exactly those reasons before the fix existed.

## ADR 0114

Read it; it does not gate this change. It governs adding or promoting a check into the required `Verified` vote aggregate in `.github/workflows/gerrit-verify.yaml`. Neither `fmt` nor `plan` here is in that aggregate (grep of `gerrit-verify.yaml` for `terraform` returns nothing), so this workflow cannot lock its own repair or revert out of the landing path — the self-lock ADR 0114 exists to prevent is unreachable here. Its *spirit* did shape the design though: the formatting signal is deliberately demoted out of the drift verdict's path rather than left blocking, which is the same restraint one step earlier.

## Not done

`terraform validate` still precedes `plan` in the same job, deliberately. Unlike fmt it is a genuine precondition: an invalid configuration cannot be planned at all, so failing there is not a missed plan, it is an impossible one. Noted in the workflow comment so a future reader does not "fix" it by symmetry.

Nothing was applied. `terraform apply` remains operator-only.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
**Patchset 2 pushed** to Gerrit change 2658 (`939dab422518`), rebased onto current `origin/main` (`084e753d30df`). Change-Id preserved.

Addresses the `iac` advisory on `.github/workflows/terraform-drift.yml`: `id-token: write` moved from the workflow top level onto the `plan` job that actually exchanges it.

I checked the convention before changing it, as asked. Every other workflow here that assumes an OIDC role scopes the grant to the job: `external-integration.yml` (two jobs), `reconcile-bridge.yml`, `structured-output-baseline.yml`, `release.yml`. `terraform-drift.yml` was the sole outlier. `release.yml` goes further and depends on that scoping for a security property — its `mcp_verify` job deliberately holds no `id-token` so an unverified binary can never run under the publishing identity.

Worth noting this advisory got sharper because of my own change: the top-level grant now also handed the token to the new `fmt` job, which makes no AWS call at all. Splitting the jobs turned a workflow-wide grant into a genuinely over-broad one.

The top-level `permissions:` block is removed entirely rather than trimmed to `contents: read`, since both jobs now declare their own explicit blocks (`fmt`: `contents: read`; `plan`: `contents: read` + `id-token: write`).

Pinned by `test_oidc_token_is_scoped_to_the_job_that_exchanges_it` in `tests/unit/test_terraform_drift_workflow_shape.py`, which asserts three things: no workflow-level `id-token`, the plan job declares it, and **no other job holds it** — so a future job cannot inherit or acquire the token without tripping the test. RED against patchset 1, verified in a throwaway worktree at the old commit.

Local state: `make lint` green (complexity `new=0 increased=0`; mechanism `new=0 increased=0 stale=0`), `make typecheck` green, terraform/drift/mechanism/workflow selection 1395 passed. One unrelated failure appeared in that run — `tests/unit/workflow/test_gate_error_sidecar.py` raised `GateCongestedError: all 4 concurrent slots busy`, a gate-admission collision with the two `review-plan` runs in flight elsewhere. It passes on its own re-run; it touches nothing in this change and is not a defect I introduced.

Orchestrator close — acceptance criteria ticked on the implementing agent's REPORTED per-AC
evidence, and the change is merged to `origin/main`.

What I verified myself before ticking:
- the merge commit exists on `origin/main` and carries this ticket's `rebar-ticket:` trailer;
- the commit is reachable from a throwaway worktree checked out at `origin/main`, which is where
  this close is being run (the shared main checkout holds another session's uncommitted work, so
  it was deliberately not fast-forwarded);
- both Gerrit gates were green on the submitted patchset (`LLM-Review +1` and `Verified +1`).

What I did NOT independently re-run: the per-AC commands. Those were executed and their output
pasted by the implementing agent, and CI re-ran the full suite on the patchset. Recording the
distinction so the trail says which evidence is first-hand and which is relayed — the completion
verifier gate is the independent check on the criteria themselves.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
THE FIX WORKED, and it proved itself within one hour of merging. Recording the first honest drift
report this workflow has produced in days.

## Before and after, from the run record

Change 2658 merged as `1f1ecea07307`. The very next scheduled Terraform Drift run
(`33950205876`, 06:34 UTC):

    job "fmt"   -> SUCCESS
    job "plan"  -> FAILURE at step "terraform plan (fail on drift)", exit code 2

Compare the three runs before the fix: the whole run died in **22-29 seconds** at `fmt -check`
and `plan` NEVER EXECUTED. Now `fmt` passes in its own job and `plan` actually runs — which is the
entire point of splitting them, and the reason the exit code is now a drift verdict rather than a
formatting complaint.

## What it found

    aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.var_tmp_cleanup_not_active   will be created
    aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.var_tmp_usage_high           will be created
    aws_instance.gerrit                                      will be updated in-place
        user_data  73abb917c5322e67... -> c8bc65ae948d1a...

These are **story S4's own alarms** (`2ba3-bf77`, "Bound /var/tmp growth and alarm on tmp
saturation"), which merged roughly an hour before this run and have not been applied.

## Why this is the exact failure this ticket was filed for

This ticket exists because story S1 declared a dedicated gate-scratch EBS volume, its attachment
and two alarms — and **none of them were ever applied**, and nobody knew for two days, because
`fmt -check` was aborting the run before `plan` could say so. That is now tracked separately as
`renowned-corked-hapuku` (`dcc3-75ee-26ce-4840`), where the volume is still attached-but-raw.

S4 has just reproduced the same shape: declared alarms, not applied. The difference is that this
time the workflow said so **within the hour**, unprompted, instead of the condition accumulating
silently. That is the whole value of the change and it is now demonstrated on live infrastructure
rather than argued from a test.

## Action arising, deliberately NOT taken in this comment

The two alarms are non-disruptive to create. The `aws_instance.gerrit` update is not: changing
`user_data` on a running EC2 instance requires a STOP/START, and the plan shows `public_ip` and
`public_dns` going to `(known after apply)`. So an unscoped apply would take Gerrit down and
potentially move its address. Noting the split rather than acting on it here; any apply should be
scoped, and the instance half is an operator-timed decision, not a drift-remediation reflex.

Also worth stating plainly: `user_data` only takes effect at boot, so applying that half changes
nothing operationally until the instance is next started — the stop/start IS the change, not a
side effect of it.

compiled_state.description:
## The defect

The scheduled **Terraform Drift** workflow runs `terraform fmt -check` as its FIRST step, before
`terraform plan`. `fmt -check` exits non-zero on any formatting deviation, so a purely cosmetic
whitespace difference aborts the job and **`terraform plan` never executes**. The workflow's
entire purpose — detecting infrastructure that has drifted from, or was never applied to match,
the declared configuration — is silently skipped.

VERIFIED from run history on `main`:

```
2026-09-04T06:39 UTC  Terraform Drift  FAILURE  22s    (sha 6b034b9f)
2026-09-03T06:40 UTC  Terraform Drift  FAILURE  29s    (sha 3e04025b)
2026-09-02T06:44 UTC  Terraform Drift  success  6m07s
```

Failure log (run 33845247102):
```
plan  terraform fmt -check   monitoring_9ea3.tf
plan  terraform fmt -check   ##[error]Process completed with exit code 3.
```

Note the durations: 22s and 29s versus 6m07s for the successful run. The short runtime is the
signature — the job died before doing any real work.

## What it cost

This is not hypothetical. While drift detection was blinded, story S1 of epic 6202 landed code
declaring a dedicated gate-scratch EBS volume, its attachment, and two CloudWatch alarms — and
**none of them were ever applied**. The volume does not exist in AWS or in Terraform state; the
live metric `gate_scratch_mounted` has read 0 on all 51 datapoints since it began publishing,
never once 1. Gates continued writing scratch to the root filesystem, which is the exact state
ADR 0112 exists to prevent.

**Drift detection is the control that would have reported those declared-but-unapplied
resources, and a whitespace nit switched it off for two days.** The story closed green on code
evidence in the meantime.

## The general shape

This is the "absence of execution reported as success/failure without anyone noticing WHAT did
not run" class that has now recurred repeatedly in this repo (9a17's worker kill, 90c7's vacuous
vote, 1ef8's vacuously-passing AC3, docker-storage-cap's SIGHUP reload reporting a cap "in
effect"). Here the run did go red, so it was not falsely green — but it went red for a cosmetic
reason that reads as trivial, and nothing distinguished "formatting is off" from "we have not
looked for drift in 48 hours".

## Current status

The formatting fix has landed: `cad66dd237cc` "Format monitoring_9ea3.tf to satisfy fmt gate"
(2026-09-04 09:54 UTC, present on origin/main). `terraform fmt -check -recursive infra/terraform`
now exits 0 locally. The next scheduled run (~2026-09-05 06:40 UTC) should clear fmt and reach
`plan` — **but that has not yet been observed**, and when it does run it should report the two
missing gate-scratch resources as drift.

So the immediate blockage is cleared. This ticket is about the ORDERING, which is unchanged and
will do the same thing the next time any `.tf` file is misformatted.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC1 — A formatting-only defect in any `infra/terraform/*.tf` file no longer prevents
      `terraform plan` from running in the Drift workflow. Prove it with a run (or a test
      harness) in which `fmt -check` would fail and `plan` still executes and reports.
- [x] AC2 — A formatting failure is still SURFACED, not silently dropped. Whatever the fix
      (reorder, `continue-on-error` with an explicit later gate, split into independent jobs),
      the run must still tell an operator that formatting is wrong.
- [x] AC3 — Drift findings and formatting findings are DISTINGUISHABLE in the run's outcome, so
      "we did not look for drift" can never again be indistinguishable from "whitespace is
      wrong". A reader must be able to tell which occurred without opening logs.
- [x] AC4 — A test or documented check pins AC1, so a future edit cannot silently restore the
      blocking order.

## Non-goals

Not changing what drift is checked, not changing alarm or volume definitions, and not applying
any Terraform — `terraform apply` is operator-only. This ticket is purely about the workflow's
step ordering and result legibility.
